newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine January inflation at 5.36 pct - poll.
newsitem.headline: Philippine January inflation at 5.36 pct - poll.

text.p: The Philippines year-on-year inflation in January is likely to be 5.36 percent compared with 11.2 percent in January 1996, according to a Reuters poll.
Six analysts polled by Reuters last week said an increase in oil prices announced in mid-January would take the inflation rate higher than December's 5.1 percent.
The government will announce January's inflation figures on Wednesday.
On January 16, the government's Energy Regulatory Board raised prices of all petroleum products by an average of 26 centavos per litre.
"The current inflation is artificially high because it merely reflects the impact of oil deregulation," said Jose Salceda, director of brokerage SBC Warburg.

Since August last year, the government implemented a new oil pricing mechanism that would change local prices each month based on changes in Singapore posted prices until full deregulation takes place in February.
Analysts say they are more worried about the inflation picture in February due to the twin effects of the oil deregulation and an increase in minimum wages.

On January 21, a government wage panel decided to raise the present minimum wage of 165 pesos in the capital by 20 pesos. The first 15 peso-increase will take effect on February and the next five pesos on May 1.
"It would be a double whammy. That may create inflationary expectations. That's unsettling for me," said Paul Joseph Garcia, an economist at Metropolitan Bank and Trust Co.

With full deregulation, the three oil refiners in the country would have to bear the foreign exchange risks for their oil imports. Previously, the government protected domestic prices by assuming those risks.
"We don't have sophisticated financial markets, such as futures, which would make the risk difficult to measure," said Manuel Ghoseco, an economist at Dharmala Securities.
Nevertheless, analysts said inflation this year would be at a lower 6.42 percent against 8.4 percent in 1996. The government has forecast a full-year inflation figure for 1997 at six to 6.5 percent.
Last year's inflation had five months of double-digit rates induced by rice shortfalls, analysts said.

And food prices, which comprise 58.5 percent of the consumer price index, are not expected to rise because the government is prepared to import 300,000 to 500,000 tonnes of rice and 500,000 tonnes of corn this year, they said.
Moreover, the country's open economy will foster competition and discourage local producers from raising prices sharply, economists said.

Socio-economic Planning Secretary Cielito Habito had said the forecast inflation in 1997 takes into account the impact of higher wages and the oil deregulation. If not for these factors, full-year inflation would have been projected at five percent, he added.

Central Bank governor Gabriel Singson said an increase of one peso in fuel prices would result in an increase in inflation of 0.1 to 0.2 percentage point and a wage increase of 20 pesos would add 0.1 percentage point.
Following are the inflation projections of analysts for January and for the full year (in percentage terms):
January (year/year) 1997
Dharmala Securities 4.9-5.3 6.2-6.5
F.Yap Securities 5.2 5.0-6.5
Metrobank 5.5 6.5
Peregrine Securities 4.5-5.0 5.9
SBC Warburg 5.2 6.0
Union Bank 6.3-6.5 8.0
Average 5.36 6.42
